title: The Binomial and Normal Distributions
description: Discrete random variables, the binomial distribution, the normal distribution, standardising and the inverse normal

notes.heading: Discrete Random Variables and Expectation
notes.body:
A **discrete random variable** $X$ takes a finite list of values, each with a probability. The **expected value** (mean) is
$$E(X) = \sum x\,P(X = x)$$
and the **variance** is
$$\operatorname{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - \big[E(X)\big]^2$$
where $E(X^2) = \sum x^2 P(X = x)$.

💡 **Worked Example** — $X$ takes values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3.
$$E(X) = 1(0.2) + 2(0.5) + 3(0.3) = 2.1$$
$$E(X^2) = 1(0.2) + 4(0.5) + 9(0.3) = 4.9 \;\Longrightarrow\; \operatorname{Var}(X) = 4.9 - 2.1^2 = 0.49$$

📌 Probabilities in a distribution table always total 1; if they do not, the table is incomplete and the missing probability must be found first.

notes.heading: The Binomial Distribution
notes.body:
The binomial model counts the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Write
$$X \sim B(n, p)$$
and then
$$P(X = r) = \binom{n}{r} p^r (1-p)^{n-r}$$

The four conditions to state or check are: a fixed number $n$ of trials; two outcomes (success or failure) each time; a constant probability $p$; and independence between trials.

💡 **Worked Example** — A fair coin is tossed 4 times. With $X \sim B(4, 0.5)$:
$$P(X = 2) = \binom{4}{2}(0.5)^2(0.5)^2 = 6 \times 0.0625 = 0.375$$

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Using the binomial when $p$ changes between trials. Drawing without replacement from a small population changes $p$, and the binomial model no longer applies.

notes.heading: Mean and Variance of a Binomial
notes.body:
For $X \sim B(n, p)$ the formulas are on the formula booklet:
$$E(X) = np \qquad \operatorname{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

💡 **Worked Example** — For $X \sim B(20, 0.3)$:
$$E(X) = 20 \times 0.3 = 6 \qquad \operatorname{Var}(X) = 20(0.3)(0.7) = 4.2$$

📌 The variance is largest when $p = 0.5$ and shrinks towards zero as $p$ approaches 0 or 1 — a useful sanity check on an answer.

🔑 These formulas work backwards too. Given the mean and $n$, divide to find $p$: a mean of 12 from 40 trials gives $p = 0.3$.

notes.heading: The Normal Distribution
notes.body:
A **continuous** random variable with a normal distribution is written
$$X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$$
where $\mu$ is the mean and $\sigma^2$ the **variance** (so the second number is not the standard deviation). The curve is bell-shaped and symmetric about $x = \mu$, with total area 1 underneath it, and probabilities are areas.

Key consequences of the symmetry:
• $P(X < \mu) = P(X > \mu) = 0.5$.
• $P(X > \mu + a) = P(X < \mu - a)$ for any $a$.
• Median and mode both equal the mean.

💡 **Worked Example** — $X \sim N(20, 16)$ has mean 20 and standard deviation $\sqrt{16} = 4$. Then $P(X > 20) = 0.5$ by symmetry, and $P(X > 24) = P(X < 16)$.

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Reading the second parameter as the standard deviation. $N(20, 16)$ has $\sigma = 4$, not 16.

notes.heading: Standardising and the Inverse Normal
notes.body:
Every normal variable can be converted to the **standard normal** $Z \sim N(0, 1)$ by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation:
$$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$
The $z$-value says how many standard deviations $x$ sits from the mean, and the area to the left of it is unchanged by the transformation.

💡 **Worked Example** — $X \sim N(20, 16)$, so $\sigma = 4$. For $x = 26$:
$$z = \dfrac{26 - 20}{4} = 1.5$$
so $P(X < 26) = P(Z < 1.5) \approx 0.933$.

💡 **The inverse normal** — Given a probability, find the value. If $P(X < a) = 0.9$ with $\mu = 50$ and $\sigma = 8$, the inverse normal gives $z = 1.2816$ and therefore
$$a = \mu + z\sigma = 50 + 1.2816(8) \approx 60.25$$

📌 A GDC does both directions directly: normalcdf for probabilities, and invNorm for values. Always sketch the curve and shade the region first, so you can tell whether the answer should be above or below the mean.

illustration.alt: A normal curve with the mean and one standard deviation either side marked, the tail beyond one standard deviation shaded, the standardising transformation shown, and a panel of binomial conditions, formulas and an example.
illustration.caption: The tail area is the probability, and subtracting the mean then dividing by σ converts any normal variable into the standard one.

notes.heading: Working Backwards with a Distribution
notes.body:
Questions often supply a probability and ask for a parameter. The method is to translate the sentence into a probability statement, then use the inverse function.

💡 **Finding a binomial parameter** — A random variable $X \sim B(10, p)$ has $P(X = 0) = 0.35$. Then
$$(1-p)^{10} = 0.35 \;\Longrightarrow\; 1 - p = 0.35^{0.1} \approx 0.9006 \;\Longrightarrow\; p \approx 0.099$$

💡 **Finding a normal parameter** — If $X \sim N(\mu, 25)$ and $P(X > 30) = 0.2$, then $\sigma = 5$ and the $z$-value with area 0.8 to its left is $0.8416$, so $30 = \mu + 0.8416(5)$ and $\mu \approx 25.8$.

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Using the given probability as the area to the left when the question describes an area to the right. Sketch first, then convert with $P(X > a) = 1 - P(X < a)$.

notes.heading: Choosing the Right Model, and Exam Technique
notes.body:
**Which model?**
• Counting successes in a fixed number of independent trials with constant $p$ — binomial, $B(n, p)$.
• A measurement that clusters symmetrically about a mean with spread — normal, $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$.
• A single event with no fixed number of trials, or a changing $p$ — neither model applies without more work.

**Exam technique**
• State the distribution before calculating, e.g. $X \sim B(12, 0.25)$, then the command you used.
• Give probabilities to 3 significant figures unless told otherwise.
• For "at least" or "at most" questions, write the inequality as a sum of equalities, or use the complement to shorten it.
• For inverse-normal questions, state the $z$-value as well as the final answer when the question asks for working.

⚠️ **Common mistakes** — Treating a normal variable as discrete; using $\sigma$ where $\sigma^2$ belongs; and forgetting that the binomial needs a fixed number of trials before it can be applied at all.

questions.stem: A discrete random variable $X$ takes the values 1, 2 and 3 with probabilities $0.2$, $0.5$ and $0.3$. Find $E(X)$.
Which of these is a condition for a binomial distribution?
choices: the probability of success is constant
the number of trials is unlimited
questions.explanation: A binomial model needs a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant probability of success and independence between trials.

questions.stem: For a normal distribution, what is $P(X > \mu)$?
questions.explanation: The normal curve is symmetric about its mean, so half the area lies above the mean: $P(X > \mu) = 0.5$.

questions.stem: For $X \sim B(20, 0.3)$, find $E(X)$.
For $X \sim B(20, 0.3)$, find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
A fair coin is tossed 4 times. Find the probability of exactly 2 heads.
Given $X \sim N(20, 16)$, find the standardised value $z$ corresponding to $x = 26$.
questions.explanation: The variance is 16, so $\sigma = 4$. Then $z = \dfrac{26 - 20}{4} = 1.5$.

questions.stem: For $X \sim N(20, 16)$, find $P(X > 24)$ to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: $\sigma = 4$, so 24 is one standard deviation above the mean. $P(Z > 1) = 1 - 0.8413 = 0.159$ to 3 s.f.

questions.stem: For $X \sim B(5, 0.1)$, find $P(X = 0)$ to 3 significant figures.
For $X \sim B(5, 0.1)$, find $P(X \ge 1)$ to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Using the complement, $P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - 0.9^5 = 0.40951 \approx 0.410$.

questions.stem: Given $X \sim N(50, 64)$ and $P(X < a) = 0.9$, find $a$ to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: $\sigma = 8$ and the $z$-value with area 0.9 to its left is 1.2816, so $a = 50 + 1.2816(8) = 60.2528 \approx 60.3$.

questions.stem: For $X \sim B(10, 0.4)$, find $P(X \ge 8)$ to 3 significant figures.
A discrete random variable has $E(X) = 2$ and $E(X^2) = 5$. Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
questions.explanation: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = 5 - 2^2 = 1$.

questions.stem: Given $X \sim N(50, 4)$, find $P(48 < X < 52)$ to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: $\sigma = 2$, so $x = 48$ and $x = 52$ correspond to $z = -1$ and $z = 1$. Then $P(-1 < Z < 1) = 0.6827 \approx 0.683$.

questions.stem: A binomial random variable $X \sim B(40, p)$ has mean 12. Find $p$.
questions.explanation: The mean of a binomial is $np$, so $40p = 12$ and $p = 0.3$.

questions.stem: A discrete random variable $X$ takes the values 0, 1 and 2 with probabilities $0.3$, $0.4$ and $0.3$. Find $E(X)$.
Which situation BREAKS the conditions for a binomial model?
choices: Rolling a fair die 20 times and counting sixes
Testing 30 bulbs from a large production line
Drawing 5 cards without replacement and counting hearts
questions.explanation: Without replacement the probability of a heart changes after each draw, so $p$ is not constant. The other situations have a fixed $n$, two outcomes, constant $p$ and independence.

questions.stem: For $X \sim N(50, 9)$, find $P(X < 50)$.
questions.explanation: The curve is symmetric about $\mu = 50$, so half the area lies below the mean: $P(X < 50) = 0.5$.

questions.stem: For $X \sim B(40, 0.25)$, find $E(X)$.
For $X \sim B(30, 0.4)$, find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
questions.explanation: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = np(1-p) = 30(0.4)(0.6) = 7.2$. ($12$ is the mean $np$; $4.8$ squares the wrong factor.)

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled 3 times. Find the probability of exactly 2 sixes.
questions.explanation: With $X \sim B\left(3, \dfrac16\right)$, $P(X = 2) = \binom32 \left(\dfrac16\right)^2 \left(\dfrac56\right) = 3 \times \dfrac{5}{216} = \dfrac{15}{216} \approx 0.0694$. ($0.0231$ forgets the factor $\binom32$; $0.421$ is $P(X \ge 1)$.)

questions.stem: Given $X \sim N(40, 9)$, find the standardised value $z$ corresponding to $x = 46$.
questions.explanation: The variance is 9, so $\sigma = 3$. Then $z = \dfrac{46 - 40}{3} = 2$. (Using $\sigma = 9$ gives the distractor $0.667$.)

questions.stem: For $X \sim N(100, 225)$, find $P(X > 130)$ to 3 significant figures.
For $X \sim B(4, 0.2)$, find $P(X = 0)$ to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: $P(X = 0) = (0.8)^4 = 0.4096 \approx 0.410$ to 3 s.f. ($0.0016$ is $0.2^4$ — the wrong probability raised to the power.)

questions.stem: For $X \sim B(6, 0.15)$, find $P(X \ge 1)$ to 3 significant figures.
Given $X \sim N(80, 25)$ and $P(X < a) = 0.75$, find $a$ to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: $\sigma = 5$ and the $z$-value with area 0.75 to its left is $0.6745$, so $a = 80 + 0.6745(5) = 83.37 \approx 83.4$. ($76.6$ comes from shading the wrong tail.)

questions.stem: For $X \sim B(12, 0.3)$, find $P(X \ge 6)$ to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: $P(X \ge 6) = P(X = 6) + P(X = 7) + \cdots + P(X = 12) = 0.0792 + 0.0291 + \cdots = 0.1178 \approx 0.118$ to 3 s.f. ($0.0792$ is only the single term $P(X = 6)$; $0.276$ wrongly starts the sum at 5.)

questions.stem: A discrete random variable has $E(X) = 3$ and $E(X^2) = 11$. Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
questions.explanation: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = 11 - 3^2 = 11 - 9 = 2$. ($8$ forgets to square the mean.)

questions.stem: Given $X \sim N(30, 4)$, find $P(27 < X < 33)$ to 3 significant figures.
A binomial random variable $X \sim B(60, p)$ has mean 15. Find $p$.
questions.explanation: The mean of a binomial is $np$, so $60p = 15$ and $p = 0.25$.
